issues.item: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study' directly conflicts with 'Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts' within the same maladaptive strategies node. Excessive work engagement and avoidance of work/study are opposing coping patterns and, without any qualifier distinguishing contexts, are clinically contradictory.

vignette: Mara is a 19-year-old Oceania woman who works as a fisherman. She has been in a relationship for over two years and recently experienced a traumatic event where she witnessed another person being severely injured. Since then, Mara has struggled with intense fear and guilt that have significantly impacted her daily life. The trauma began one day while working on the boat. Mara had just finished checking some fishing nets when she heard screams from the shore. Rushing over, she found a man bleeding profusely after falling from a cliff. Despite her attempts to help him, he did not survive. The vivid memory of his pain and suffering has haunted her ever since. Mara now experiences intense triggers in various forms that remind her of this traumatic event. Hearing footsteps behind or nearby on the beach makes her heart race as she fears another person might be in danger again. Similarly, any sound reminiscent of the commotion on that day sends waves of panic through her body. The mere sight of a bicycle can trigger flashbacks, reminding her of how quickly things went wrong that fateful day. These triggers have led Mara to develop several maladaptive strategies as coping mechanisms. She often works excessively long hours to avoid being alone with her thoughts and the memories they evoke. Spending extended periods on her phone or playing games provides a temporary escape from the haunting images and emotions. However, this constant distraction only serves to delay the inevitable intrusion of painful recollections. When Mara remembers the event, she experiences intense guilt for not preventing what happened. She feels that her body reacts before her mind can process danger, leaving her constantly vigilant and fearful. This heightened state of alertness leads her to assume something bad is happening whenever there's a delay or unexpected situation, further exacerbating her anxiety. Her memory often forces itself into her consciousness without warning, sometimes leaving her feeling the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image. The guilt she feels during these moments makes it difficult for her to concentrate on anything else, leading her to believe that her body keeps reacting as if she is still in danger even when she is safe. The fear that she will not be able to control her anger and do something terrible adds another layer of distress. She has come to believe that her failure to protect others during the traumatic event means she is fundamentally flawed, and this belief has reinforced her maladaptive coping strategies. She avoids intimate situations with her partner, fearing that her intense emotions might lead to harmful actions. Over time, Mara's avoidance behaviors have taken a toll on both her work and personal life. Her excessive hours at sea have strained her relationship, as she often comes home exhausted and emotionally drained. The constant distraction from technology has also become a significant barrier in maintaining close connections with others. What finally brought Mara to seek help was the realization that these coping mechanisms were no longer working. She was certain that she needed support to manage her intense emotions and fears effectively. Despite her reservations, she hopes that therapy can provide her with tools to break this cycle of distress and regain control over her life.
